summary: This informational RFC describes considerations for moving end-user content, typically web-based, to IPv6. It explores challenges and migration tactics, and may apply to other services.

eli5.summary: If you run a website, how do you get ready for the new internet addresses? This lists the steps and troubles.

questions: how to enable ipv6 for web content
how to move website to ipv6
subtitle: Strategies for gradually moving web services to IPv6 addressing

tldr.problem: Content providers face technical, operational, and capacity challenges when moving their web services to IPv6, including impaired access for some users and the need to gradually manage traffic volume.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6589 describes migration tactics including IPv6-specific test domains, DNS resolver whitelisting (returning IPv6 addresses only to prepared networks), and direct dual-stack deployment, with phased implementation approaches.
tldr.outcome: Content providers can incrementally transition to IPv6 while maintaining service quality, though the RFC notes this is informational guidance rather than a prescriptive standard.

facts.label: Whitelist approach
facts.value: Returns AAAA records only to known-good DNS resolvers

facts.label: Blacklist approach
facts.value: Returns AAAA records to all except networks with known issues

facts.label: Key management method
facts.value: Authoritative DNS server checks resolver IP address

today: RFC 6589 is an Informational document that remains relevant for organizations planning IPv6 adoption. It has not been obsoleted, though real-world IPv6 deployment has evolved since its publication in April 2012, with higher adoption rates and fewer impairment issues reported over time.

sections.title: Transitioning Web Content to IPv6
sections.content:
As the Internet runs out of IPv4 addresses, content providers must move their websites and services to IPv6. RFC 6589 focuses on the practical challenges and solutions for this transition, especially for high-traffic websites that serve millions of users.

The document acknowledges that not all domains face the same challenges. A small website might be able to switch immediately, but major search engines, social networks and news sites need careful planning to avoid disrupting users who might experience slow or broken connections.
sections.eli5: Big websites need a plan to switch to the new addresses without breaking things for their visitors. Small sites can switch faster.

sections.title: Challenges in IPv6 Adoption
sections.content:
Three main challenges affect the transition. First, IPv6-related impairment: studies found that about 0.078% of internet users have configuration problems on their devices or networks that cause slow or failed connections when given IPv6 addresses. For a massive website, even this small fraction means thousands of affected users.

Second, operational immaturity: network operations teams and monitoring systems are less experienced with IPv6 than IPv4, creating risk when traffic suddenly shifts. Third, volume concerns: high-traffic sites must manage the risk that opening IPv6 all at once could overwhelm networks or expose latent problems.
sections.eli5: Some computers have trouble with IPv6 connections. Networks are still learning how to run IPv6. And switching everyone at once could cause big problems.

sections.title: Transition Strategies
sections.content:
RFC 6589 describes several tactics. IPv6-specific names like ipv6.example.com let early adopters test while keeping regular traffic on IPv4. This builds operational experience with low risk.

DNS Resolver Whitelisting is more sophisticated: the authoritative DNS server checks which recursive resolver made the query. It returns IPv6 addresses (AAAA records) only to resolvers on a whitelist of known-good networks, preventing impaired users from receiving broken IPv6 records. Domains can manually maintain the whitelist, or automate it as networks prove their IPv6 readiness.

DNS Blacklisting inverts this: all networks get IPv6 by default, except a blacklist of networks with known problems. This requires less operational work and is useful as IPv6 maturity improves.

Direct dual-stack deployment skips these intermediate steps and simply enables IPv6 for all users, leaving it to the users and their ISPs to resolve any impairment issues.
sections.eli5: You can: make a special test name only early adopters use; carefully pick which networks get IPv6 based on a list of good ones; block only the few broken networks; or just switch everyone at once.

sections.title: Deployment Roadmap
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a sequence of phases. A domain might start with no IPv6 access, then launch an IPv6-specific name for testing. Next, it deploys DNS whitelisting manually to control which resolvers receive IPv6 records. As operations mature, it can automate the whitelist based on measured IPv6 readiness. Later, it switches to blacklisting only the problematic networks. Finally, it reaches full dual-stack, where all users can access the content over IPv4 or IPv6.

Each domain follows its own path; some skip phases, and others move at different speeds based on their user base, traffic volume, and operational readiness.
sections.eli5: You start with just IPv4, test with a special name, carefully give out IPv6 to good networks, then take away IPv6 from bad networks, and finally let everyone use IPv6.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
If a domain uses whitelisting or blacklisting, it must protect the configuration from unauthorized changes that could disrupt traffic or expose the system to attack. DNSSEC signing still works with these DNS policies; the authoritative server can sign both the positive response (IPv6 records) and the negative response (non-existence), so DNS security is maintained.

When collecting or publishing statistics about IPv6 impairment rates, domains should never disclose individual users or detailed data that could identify them. Aggregate statistics like 'our domain saw 0.05% impairment in September' protect privacy.

A special concern arises when users have much better IPv6 connectivity than IPv4 (for example, because their ISP has run out of IPv4 addresses and uses large-scale NAT). A domain that blocks IPv6 for those users could actually make their experience worse.
sections.eli5: Keep the DNS settings safe from hackers. Don't reveal individual user information when sharing impairment data. Sometimes a user's IPv6 is better than IPv4, so be careful about blocking IPv6.
